speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1990-91 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak at the third reading stage of an important bill that provides the government with the necessary borrowing authority so that it can proceed with its operations. At this point, I think it would be useful to recall some of the historic and economic highlights of the years since 1984, when the Conservative government was elected.
As you know, one of the government's major initiatives was the economic message tabled by the Minister of Finance in November 1984, in which the government set out its economic policies for the years to come. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that this message mentioned being competitive, reducing the national debt and of course our annual deficit, and creating jobs. It mentioned opening up our country for trade. Since 1984, the unemployment rate has gone down, and job creation has improved considerably, not only in terms of the number of jobs created but also in terms of their quality. You will recall that before that time, 80 per cent of the jobs
created were for a limited term: programs to build or paint fences, clean windows and do general repairs, while 80 per cent of the jobs created by this government since 1984 are permanent jobs. These are jobs where women have their share of the market. This is another innovation that did not exist before 1984.
The economic message of the Minister of Finance mentioned trade. As you know, Mr. Speaker, this government negotiated and finalized the free trade agreement, and in November 1988, Canadians also finalized the free trade issue by electing a majority Tory government, the only party that supported free trade, a matter of vital importance for the future of this country. Without wishing to expand on the free trade debate, I think it is important to point out that in an economy like Canada's, we must have secure access to markets outside Canada. That is what free trade has done, by removing tariff barriers between Canada and the United States.
Mr. Speaker, the free trade agreement was also important because we had to ensure that Canadian companies would be able to export to the United States, without the tariff barriers we have faced, in certain cases, between 1984 and 1988, and I am thinking of cedar shingles and shakes, for instance. Of course, free trade was also an integral part of the economic policies of the Minister of Finance in November 1984. There was the issue of our national debt which, as we all know, was $200 billion in 1984. And that is too much, far to much. In 1984, the annual deficit was $39 billion, which means that in 1984, this government, spent $39 billion more than it collected in revenues. Imagine if a Canadian family, whatever its income, spent $39,000 more than it earned in a year, and that this was added to the $200,000 it had already overspent. This family would definitely go bankrupt.
Since 1984, we have had to apply draconian measures to existing programs, to planned government investment in various areas and to the federal Public Service. We had to make decisions that were not necessarily popular, in order to reduce government spending and thus reduce the annual deficit which had reached alarming propor-

May 14, 1990

tions, continued to increase each year and unfortunately still continues to add to the national debt.
In 1984, the government spent-forget interest costs for a minute; unfortunately we cannot do that as a rule, but for the purposes of my example, let's leave out interest costs-the government spent $15 billion more that it collected in revenues, and this does not include the interest paid on the debt. The government still spent $15 billion more than the revenues it collected. This year, that same government, again excluding interest payments, will spend 9 billion less than the revenues it collects. This means that after nearly six years, government spending in all areas, whether we are talking about the public service, programs, capital spending or investment-this year, we will spend $9 billion less than what we will collect in of taxes. That is what I call good management.
However, Mr. Speaker, we still have the deficit problem. In fact, why do we have a deficit this year? The deficit exists because we have additional expenses in the form of the interest that must be paid on the debt, and the national debt was the legacy we received from the former Liberal Government in 1984. Since that time, the cumulative debt is the interest that we have to pay on the legacy we received. It is just something we have to live with, Mr. Speaker. I think Canadians are also more aware of the increasing problems created by the rising cost of this debt burden, which will mean that this year, for instance, 35 cents out of every tax dollar will go to pay interest. You can imagine what we could do as a government, with the help of the opposition, if we had those 35 cents per dollar to give to Canadians through various programs. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, as you know, we do not have it.
But, again, we are off to a good start. Interest rates and costs hurt the government, as I think everyone would admit, but at least we are managing and spending less money than we take in.
Very often, Mr. Speaker, we hear the opposition say that tax increases explain why the deficit has gone down. That, Mr. Speaker, is absolutely false, and I want to emphasize it. Seventy per cent of deficit reduction is due to government cutbacks and 30 per cent is due to tax increases since 1984. I think that is a fair balance.
Remember 1988, when we reduced the income tax on individuals. I do not remember hearing the opposition talk about that often. Obviously that is good news, Mr. Speaker.
This year we are implementing the goods and services tax, and that is good news. It is good news if it is dealt with honestly and frankly. For 66 years now, we have had a federal sales tax at the manufacturer's level. That means, Mr. Speaker, that no one, no Canadian, sees the rate of this tax and is even aware that he or she is paying this federal tax on most goods and services in the country. For 66 years, this hidden tax has meant that every year, the government collects money without Canadians being aware of it.
We are the only country in the world now that still has a federal sales tax at the manufacturer's level. However, 48 countries have already adopted a consumption tax, whether it is called a VAT or a GST. Mr. Speaker, now more than ever it is time for Canada to take its place as well and implement a progressive, fair and equitable tax system. It is hard to have a tax that is fair and equitable.
The GST meets these criteria. It will replace the present federal sales tax which is bad for Canadian taxpayers and also bad for Canadian businesses. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the federal manufacturer's sales tax favours foreign companies that send goods to Canada because they do not have to pay 13.5 per cent on the goods they produce.
Thus foreign goods have an advantage over goods produced in Canada. You know, Mr. Speaker, that makes no sense. Moreover, when a Canadian producer wants to sell abroad, his costs include a 13.5 per cent manufacturer's tax that no other country in the world has. So when he comes to sell this chair, he has a 13.5 per cent tax in his costs which his competitor in country X, Y or Z does not have. What does this Canadian producer do? He is stuck with his goods; he is unable to sell them because they cost too much.
The goods and services tax will eliminate that situation. It is a 7 per cent consumption tax that will appear on the bill the consumer pays. This means that all Canadians will know what the goods and services tax costs them whenever they spend money on something.
May 14, 1990

But even more than that, Mr. Speaker, all Canadian families whose income is $30,000 or less will receive a tax credit in advance. That is, in December 1990, the Government of Canada will send a cheque to all Canadian families whose annual income is $30,000 or less. A cheque just so the GST is fair and equitable, just so low-income families are not penalized by the implementation of a new tax. I want to point out that it was the new Conservative government which began to follow this new approach in 1986. It was the new Conservative government which in 1986 first gave a tax credit applicable to the federal sales tax. A higher credit is again given with respect to the GST, and again it goes to families that have a higher income than they did before. Again it is given so as to make the tax system fair and equitable. You will hear opposition members criticize the GST. Mr. Speaker, I dare you to recall a single instance where they came up with a fair and valid monetary alternative for Canadians after criticizing the GST. How easy it is to say that one is against higher taxes, against taxes. That is the easy way out. But this government has responsibilities in connection with the deficit, elderly people, and provincial transfers. The federal government has to collect money to meet its responsibilities and redistribute the wealth. Anyone who is against the GST has to tell me where else the $18 billion will come from so we can meet the needs of Canadians. That is the question. In that respect opposition members are not doing their job when they fail to come up with an alternative and keep saying they are against it.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I look at the riding of Trois-Ri-vieres where competition is fierce among people who sell cars, cakes or what have you. But when a dealer claims his product is better, he explains why it is so and why he sells it. When they talk about the future of the country and say that a measure tabled by the government is no good, if they are a genuine opposition party, they ought to come up with a solution. However, when we hear the opposition talk, no solutions seem to be forthcoming.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1990-91 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member will be very pleased to comment on my speech later on. I am looking forward to that.

The GST, in addition to being a fair and equitable tax, will favour exports of Canadian businesses and will benefit Canadian businesses that must compete with foreign companies that export goods to Canada. If our Canadian companies produce more, that means they need more workers. If they need more workers, that means more jobs will be created. That is how this government has been running the country since 1984. It all goes back to the economic message the Minister of Finance tabled in November 1984.
About the unemployment rate on the weekend in the riding of Trois-Rivieres, it was announced that the unemployment rate had gone down. Why did the unemployment rate go down since 1984? It went down because Canadian companies looked at the government and said: They are working very hard to run the country the way we in the private sector run a business. And when that is the case, people invest. They have confidence in the government, they invest, and that is how jobs are created. You know, Mr. Speaker, we often brag about the fact that the government creates jobs, but basically, it was the good financial climate created by the government that led Canadian businesses to invest and increase the number of jobs in this country. And I am talking about permanent jobs, not part-time, patchwork jobs. I am talking about permanent jobs in lucrative areas, in areas where women also have their share of the labour market.
Mr. Speaker, that was a summary of the highlights of what has happened since 1984, while also situating the importance of this bill in the Canadian economic context.
With your permission, I would also like to mention the deregulation of the energy and transportation industries. I could speak at length about the National Energy Program, which was a disaster for all Canadians, for Western Canadians as well as Quebecers. It was a real disaster, and we had to do a hatchet job on this program, which, I must confess, we did with considerable pleasure.
The same could be said of Investment Canada. In the transportation sector, government decisions were made which helped this sector and helped our Canadian businesses to operate well, to be more competitive, to progress, to make money and to pay their taxes.

Government Orders
We often hear the opposition say there are 50,000 or 60,000-1 am not sure how many-companies that don't pay income tax. That is false, Mr. Speaker. That is totally false. All Canadian companies pay income tax. When they do not, the reason is they don't have any tax to pay, Mr. Speaker, and that happens when a company incurs a loss. So of course it will not have to pay income tax. Any Canadian taxpayer who in 1989, for instance, earned $45,000 and in 1990 incurs a loss of $35,000, may apply the loss incurred to a previous year's or the next year's income. This is allowed under the Income Tax Act. And the same applies to companies.
Most of the many companies, if the opposition is to be believed, that do not pay income tax are, in fact, small businesses like the ones in your riding, in Trois-Rivieres, or in their ridings, which make a profit one year and lose money the next. We know, Mr. Speaker, that life isn't easy for small businesses. There are some good years, and there are years when business is slow, but the opposition wants us to tax a company that has already lost money!
The companies that make money, Mr. Speaker, pay their taxes, and they have done so since 1986, when we introduced a minimum personal tax. Every single Canadian is paying his fair share of income tax, despite all the tax shelters people can dream up or try to use. Even if they have 18,000 tax shelters, they will still have to pay their fair share of tax because we now have a minimum income tax that this government established, Mr. Speaker, at the same time it abolished the scandalous scientific research tax credits of the former government. It was a scandal. Millions of dollars were wasted, the way this scheme was organized. We put an end to it, Mr. Speaker.
Now if you want to do scientific research, there is no problem. But you still must account for these expenditures in the normal way and not according to the system brought in by former finance minister Lalonde in 1984.
So, getting back to our bill, we must consider the emphasis we have put on things like the Jobs Strategy since 1984. You will recall that before 1984, there were summer programs for students that involved painting fences and sweeping. Mr. Speaker, tell me what post-secondary or university students learned by painting fences in the summer. They learned nothing! Those programs were boondoggles.
Mr. Speaker, we established the Challenge Program which helps students do work that is partly subsidized by the federal government in their future field of activity. Last Friday in my riding, I had the opportunity to take part in the opening for the summer of the student employment centre for the ridings of Trois-Rivieres and Champlain and the person in charge of the Challenge Program pointed out the importance of this program whereby students can earn money and learn during the summer about the field in which they will eventually work. The honorary chairman, Mr. Gaulin, a dynamic young man, is in charge of personnel for a company in my riding. He pointed out how good it is for a company during the summer to have one, two, three or five young people with their new expertise and new techniques that they learned during the year. As they earn money, the young people help the company, which also helps them financially, and learn something practical. We all know that universities are wonderful places but are sometimes weak on the practical side. Thanks to the summer program, young people at the end of their university studies will graduate with a diploma and practical experience. Mr. Speaker, that is what the Challenge Program, established in 1985, does and it works very well.
With respect to employment programs, Mr. Speaker, consider job development programs for which applicants are necessarily people who want to learn something new. The organization or the employer that has such a program trains the applicant in a new sector and pays him or her. Of course the federal government is there to help pay part of the costs. This is a productive program prepared and launched under the Conservative government. Before, as I recall, there was the Canada Works program under which people were hired to shovel snow in yards. Mr. Speaker, shoveling snow in yards is hardly the way to acquire a new skill.

That was said in 1978 by a well-known professor who belonged to a Quebec accounting firm which now has offices across Canada. This professor said 12 years ago: The federal sales tax is bad for the country. That was 12 years ago, Mr. Speaker. This government got the message. Yes, we are going to change the tax system. Yes, we are going to introduce a new tax called the GST, the goods and services tax, a tax that will be paid by the consumer. That is a major change, and Canadians are worried. They are asking questions. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, when they put their questions to government members, they get good answers. When they put their questions to the opposition, the answers are less than accurate.
I think the opposition has a duty to explain the GST properly, because it should be explained. It is a major change-

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see the opposition is finally starting to react. I waited thirty-five minutes for them to react, and finally, it worked!
I repeat, the GST has the advantage that Canadians will be able to see this tax. A number of people in the beautiful riding of Trois-Rivieres told me: We trust the Conservative Government, and we know you will keep the tax at 7 per cent. But if the Liberals ever come to power, 10 or 15 years from now, they are going to raise the tax to 8, or 9 or 10 per cent. That is what the people of my riding are saying. I tell them no. The great advantage of the GST compared to the federal sales tax is that it is visible. The party in power, whether Conservative or Liberal, will be ashamed to raise it because it will appear on people's bills the next day. That is the guarantee Canadians have that this tax will stay at 7 per cent. It is a visible tax, compared to the other one at 13.5 per cent that no one sees. How much federal sales tax at
13.5	per cent did I pay on that? No idea. No one knows. The same goes for my glass and furniture. Starting January 1, 1991, we will have a visible tax, which will let everyone know what they are paying. Again, there will also be a tax credit.
The opposition cannot challenge the figures published in an article in La Presse maybe two or three weeks ago. In it, a journalist explained, for example, that a senior whose annual income is $12,000 will be in a better position with the tax credit for the federal sales tax in 1991 than that person is in 1990 with the present tax. The La Presse article has figures to back it up.
The same calculation was done for a single person earning $25,000 a year who has two children. Once again, the figures show that a single-parent family with two children would be in a better position in 1991 than in 1990. They would have more money in their pockets in 1991 with a 7 per cent GST than in 1990 with a 13.5 per cent FST. Mr. Speaker, we must talk about it; we must emphasize it. I think that the opposition members who will speak must also point out that the GST is advantageous for families earning less than $30,000. They will have more money to spend. We must say that. Some sectors of the economy will feel the benefits.

The owner of the Jean Coutu pharmacies whom I met in my riding last weekend, Mr. Speaker, was telling me: "Prices will go down next year with the GST." In the car industry also, big companies like GM and Ford with big money involved and certainly a few accountants looking into that kind of thing full time admit that cars will cost less in 1991 thanks to the GST. The Sears stores said the same thing. The goods they sell will cost less. The same for Canadian Tire. Mr. Speaker, there are nonetheless national chain stores saying: "Yes indeed, consumers will pay less once the new tax is implemented." Some will ask, and rightly so: What guaranty is there that the 13.5 per cent will be taken off? There is always competition, Mr. Speaker.
Domestic economic realities must also be considered. As we remember, when cameras first came onto the market, they cost a fortune. If we wanted a better zoom or some other feature, we needed another part. It cost an arm and a leg. Now, we can walk into any fine store and buy a camera that does everything by itself. At the push of a button, the flash, zoom and everything else work automatically, and the price is a fraction of what it used to be. For example, when color television sets were first sold in Canada 25 years ago, they cost more than today even with inflation factored in because technology is improving every year and competition is everywhere. Today we pay the same price, or even less, for a small color TV as we would have paid 25 years ago for a big one.
The competition is there. It has its place and will make the GST a viable proposition for all Canadian consumers.

The government did a marvellous job of that, an absolutely marvellous job of reducing the national debt. Indeed, if we go back and look at the national debt as it was in September 1984, or during the fiscal year when the government took over, we will find that it was in the order of $150 billion or $160 billion. I have the figure here somewhere. It was $170 billion when the government took over in September 1984.
We understand, according to the Minister of Finance then and now and according to the gentleman from Trois-Rivieres, that the undertaking was to reduce the national debt. The government reduced it all right, I say to him. He should have a talk to his speech writer. The government reduced it all the way from $170 billion down to $360 billion. How is that for reducing? That is a new definition of reduction. The government has more than doubled that national debt in six years.

It got us away from providing needed infrastructure in the fishing industry that was most beneficial in helping fishermen pursue their trade-slip ways on which to pull up their boats, wharfs to tie their boats to, stages on which to split and clean their fish.
Those people who want to knock the short-term job creation programs are very selective in how they characterize them. They always pick the painting of the cemetery fence. Yes, that was done under some of those programs, but what was done much more often under those programs-and therefore he ought not to be maligning those programs-is that good infrastructure was put in place such as wharfs and slip ways. I could mention health clinics. I could mention a Girl Guide camp in one part of my riding, a place called Jean de Baie. It is a regional Girl Guide facility used literally by thousands of Girl Guides every summer. It was built under job creation.
We could go to Marystown and see the fire tower which was built to train firemen from all over eastern Newfoundland in emergency procedures. However he chooses, instead, to talk about painting cemetery fences. I say to him that he ought not to knock what was a program that served rural people particularly very well. It served them a lot better than the present charade is serving them, where they are told they can get job creation money provided they will agree to be retrained. That is the magic word now: retrained.
Nobody in his right mind in any community in this country is against retraining, but we have to look at it in the context of some small communities in Atlantic Canada. I will pick one because it has been much in the news lately: the community of Gaultois which is in my riding on the south coast of Newfoundland. It is one community on an island called Long Island. There is no road connection from the island to the mainland of Newfoundland. My good friend, the hon. member for Willowdale, and I visited the community of Gaultois in the last week or so. He saw, as I have seen for many
years, the industry of those people. We watched them in a plant pursuing a skill that they had acquired, refined, and improved over a lifetime.
The government says that they ought to retrain. For what do you retrain people in the community of Gaultois? That is not to be condescending; it is to underline the point that those people already possess any training, any skills that they need to survive in that community. Whether it is the skill to split and clean fish or to catch fish, carpentry skills, welding skills, homemakers' skills or secretarial skills, the skills which are needed in that community are there in abundance.
Retraining in that context, in the context of the government's program, is a code word for forced resettlement. These people will have to pack their suitcases, pick up their bags, leave their homes, leave their loved ones, and go off to urban Canada.
I am looking forward to hearing the remarks of the hon. member for Simcoe Centre. She is just bursting with ideas today and as soon as I am through sometime today, tomorrow, or Wednesday-whenever I get through here-I hope she will get up and tell us her concerns about this particular bill that would have the government borrow $25.5 billion, but I digress.
I was responding to some of the points made by the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres. He also said that this government, the government of which he is a supporter, had opened up the countiy to trade interests. I would say that is putting it rather charitably. Opening up the country to trade interests is a very charitable way of stating what has happened. I would put it more bluntly and to the point: that it has sold out the countiy to certain interests.
One only has to look at the government's sweetheart deal with American Express, with Amex, to realize that one has to be a foreigner to get a deal with this government, either a foreigner or on a very short list of people who funded the Tory campaign in the last federal election. I say a short list because it did not take a very long list; if they are all throwing in money up in the millions, it does not take many contributors to fund a campaign.
I wanted to say, in response to the gentleman from Trois-Rivieres, that he should be a little more candid when he is talking about what this government has done in terms of trade interest. I say to him that beyond opening up the countiy it has sold out, particularly to
May 14, 1990

American interests. That is a theme that I would pursue if I had the time.

subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN
STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1972 each successive federal government has shown its concern for women's issues by meeting with representatives from the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. These annual meetings provide an opportunity for both NAC members and cabinet to openly discuss issues that affect all Canadian families.
The government may not always have agreed with what NAC had to say and NAC may not always have liked the way government was conducting business, but at least the lines of communication were left open. This policy has now changed. The government has now shown its contempt for women's concerns by refusing to meet publicly with the representatives of the more than 500 organizations with memberships of over three million. It has sent a clear signal to women that their concerns are not high on the Tory agenda.
This government has slashed support programs, threatened to close women's centres, ignored the day care crisis and has now turned its back on the NAC spokespersons. It is time that this government remembered that its mandate also included public accountability.

subtopic: NATIVE AWARENESS WEEK
NATIVE AWARENESS WEEK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday at Rocky Mountain House Historic Park, I was privileged to join with elected provincial and municipal politicians, along with Chief Tom Bigchild and Chief Caroline Beaverbones from the Sunchild and O'Chiese reserves to officially recognize Native Awareness Week in the province of Alberta.
Chief Caroline spoke quietly and eloquently as she, on Mother's Day, told of her pride in her children and grandchildren and her equally strong pride in her heritage.
We all spoke on the need to foster tolerance and understanding, and of the need to be proud of our heritage and our country.

May 14, 1990
The young people from the Sunchild, O'Chiese and Bighorn Reserves provided examples of that pride in art, poems and song.
My compliments go to the organizers from the Rocky Mountain House Native Friendship Centre and the parks staff who provided an opportunity for natives and non-natives to further appreciate the culture and contribution of native Canadians.

subtopic: NATIONAL TOURISM WEEK
NATIONAL TOURISM WEEK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today marks the beginning of National Tourism Awareness Week and I invite all Canadians to participate in events designed to heighten our awareness of this critical industry.
Not many people know how important tourism is to the Canadian economy. It is our third largest industry at $25 billion per year, our second largest earner of foreign exchange at $7 billion, and it contributes $11 billion in tax revenues to government. It provides employment to all regions of Canada and to all segments of the labour force. In fact, 632,000 people, or 10 per cent of the labour force, derive their living from tourism.
In the near north alone, which includes my riding of Nipissing, tourism generates $200 million annually and $1 billion across all of northern Ontario. Yet this government continues to neglect this key industry. At a time when competition for the world travel market is intensifying, we should not be tacking on an additional 7 per cent to the cost of our tourism products. Indeed, when the government sees fit to slash the tourism promotion budget from $35 million to $20 million, we have to question its commitment to this vital industry which will be the world's largest by the next decade.

STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the government is always ready to meet with its corporate friends, it has once again refused to meet with the National Action Committee on the Status of Women.
Were the government listening, it would hear a reasoned voice on the subject of peace and disarmament. Women have been at the forefront of the peace movement. Agnes Macphail, the first women MP and a member of my party, worked tirelessly for the cause of peace and international co-operation. New Democrats are proud to continue that tradition.
The NDP has been speaking out about the considerable economic advantages of peace and disarmament. Savings in defence spending will produce what has been called a peace dividend. Canadian women are demanding that these funds be used to promote improvements in the human condition. The peace dividend can and must be part of a fundamental restructuring of global priorities. Much can be achieved in the current political climate. What is required is leadership.
The time is long overdue for a complete and progressive update of our foreign and defence policy. When will this government listen to the voice of women?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MEECH LAKE ACCORD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ten years ago today then Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, at the height of the referendum debate, told a gathering in Montreal's Paul Sauve Arena that a "no" vote would lead to a renewal of federalism. The majority of Quebecers who voted no, and in fact the rest of Canada, believed that this renewed federalism would involve all provinces, including Quebec.
As we all know, in 1982 Canada patriated her Constitution. Mr. Trudeau affected a renewal of federalism. The problem was and still is that Quebec was left out.
In 1987, the Prime Minister joined all ten Premiers in drafting the Meech Lake Constitutional Accord. This accord fulfilled the promise of renewed federalism, unkept for seven years.
Ten years have passed since Quebec voted yes to Canada. Ten years have passed with Quebec out in the constitutional cold. Ten weeks have passed since I encouraged Canada's 11 First Ministers to reconsider their positions and find a way around the constitutional impasse that we now face.
May 14, 1990

There are now five weeks left to Meech. All Canadians are counting down to Meech. All Canadians are counting on Canada's First Ministers.

subtopic: JUSTICE
JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to use the next minute to implore the Minister of Justice to get a move on in the David Milgaard case.
David Milgaard has been in jail for 21 years for a murder he says he never committed and there is now serious doubt as to his guilt. Even the RCMP are interviewing a suspect in the case.
Despite the fact that the Department of Justice was asked more than a year ago to reopen the case, the file has yet to reach the desk of the minister. Why? What is behind this procrastination? Is it sloth? Is it indifference? Is it hubris? Is it the desire to protect the reputations of certain individuals?
Whatever the reason, it is now time for the Minister of Justice to act on the David Milgaard case, for justice delayed is justice denied.

STANDING COMMITTEE ON CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to inform the House of a significant development with respect to the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs. That committee, last Thursday, sent a summons to the Canadian Union of Public Employees indicating the union is an important witness in our study of the economic effects of the GST. CUPE President Jeff Rose has now responded saying he will appear before the committee next Tuesday evening.
This is an example of responsible leadership. Mr. Rose and I may disagree fundamentally on a number of issues but I would like to hold Mr. Rose up as a model of a responsible labour leader in this country and I urge every other labour leader in the country to be as responsible. I hope Shirley Carr is listening.

subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last February 15 I made some comments in this House concerning the finance ministry's provision of brochures, in one official language only, to residents of my riding concerning the goods and services tax. On May 1, I again received a letter from a constituent complaining that he had received government information concerning the GST in one language only.

The same problem also occurred throughout the Acadian peninsula where a number of people received a GST English-only publication from the Government of Canada.

How much longer must New Brunswickers wait until the federal government offers them services in both official languages?

ANTI-SEMITISM

Parliamentarians and all persons who respect human rights and abhor racism join with Jews to lament and protest such anti-Semitic acts which create fear of another holocaust and bring shame on us all.

subtopic: MEECH LAKE ACCORD
MEECH LAKE ACCORD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been over ten years since the majority of Quebecers voted no in the referendum after what was described as a major and memorable intervention by former Prime Minister of Canada Pierre Trudeau. He did assure them that no meant yes to renewed federalism, and I quote: If the answer to the referendum question is no, we all said that the no will be interpreted as a mandate to change the Constitution and renew federalism.
But after patriating the Constitution in 1982 without the agreement of Quebec, Mr. Speaker, the former Prime Minister reneged on his promise.
This is why I consider that the current Meech Lake Accord is the obvious sign of the fairness and efficiency of the constitutional program and objectives of the Prime Minister of Canada. I for one hope that he will be able to win the faith and good will of all Canadians.

subtopic: MOTHER'S DAY
MOTHER'S DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday was Mother's Day 1990. Canadians celebrate this day to show reverence to all mothers and to appreciate the sacrifices they endure for their children throughout their living years.
Lest we forget, let me quote a few lines from Susan Kastner's reflections in "Mother has Reason to Weep" which appeared in yesterday's Toronto Star.
There are mothers weeping over children who have
disappeared - ; who weep while they hold their starving children in
their laps; -who weep for daughters and sons-sold into
prostitution to get the family a little to eat; -who weep because their young are being murdered by drugs; -who weep because their children will grow up paying forever for the colour of their skin; -who weep for children sent to war; there are mothers who weep because there are no jobs for their men or for themselves, and the future holds no prospect of jobs for their children.
Yes, mothers continue to think of their children and men. We in Parliament should think always of all mothers and of those for whom they weep.

STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has become obvious to even the most casual observer that the priorities of this government are misplaced.
The Minister responsible for the Status of Women and her colleague, the Secretary of State, are making much of the reinstated funding for women's centres, but this action betrays the shallowness of this government's commitment to women in Canada.
Bill C-69 will limit funding transfers for child care, for shelter for battered women, for income support. That is the Tory commitment to women and children in this country.
Women and their children are the victims of this government's misplaced priorities. It has cut the Canada Assistance Plan, it has cut UI coverage, it has clawed back old age pensions and it has clawed back family allowance. This government has no commitment to women's equity. It has no commitment to children. Its priorities are misplaced and wrongheaded and Canadian women will neither forgive nor forget this government for its insistent attack upon them.

FISHERIES
speechtext:

May 14, 1990

speechtext:

With respect to the province of Quebec, the Minister of Fisheries is prepared to discuss with the province of Quebec whatever program may be particularly needed in that province.
In addition, this program concentrates on the problems of the fishery, particularly with respect to the offshore and in connection with the total allowable catches that were recommended as a result of scientific advice and the interim report of the Harris committee this year.

speechtext: Taken away from other programs.

speechtext:

Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International
Trade): Mr. Speaker, the lobster season has really just begun in its fullest sense at the present time. There is a problem with lobster because there is an over-supply in so far as the markets are concerned.

Various fairs, missions and market intelligence activities are planned to enhance the diversification of processed lobster to encourage the development of new products in an attempt to overcome this problem, which is not a simple one because it is a problem of over-supply.

May 14, 1990

best health of all those on the Island of Montreal, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:

subtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED

It points out that it is a tremendously unfair tax on the basis that it is regressive in that it is taxing people who are least able to afford this kind of tax. That is not what 80 per cent of Canadians are saying. They are saying the opposite, that it is the most regressive and unfair tax. speechtext:
The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres said that the Liberals have no alternative to the goods and services tax. First, the role of an opposition is to point out what is less than perfect about the government's policies. On the goods and services tax, we have had no difficulty whatsoever finding some imperfections. If we had done no more than that, we would have served our role as Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition.
Being the thinkers we are, we went a step further. We knew those big, bad Tories are going to suggest, that we have no alternative. We went out and got a few alternatives. Let me outline them for the sake of debate?

May 14, 1990
Government Orders
First, we said that a consumption tax ought to be fair. We are not the only people who say that. The Minister of Finance said it back in 1984. He said that the first principle of a tax is that it ought to be fair. We stand by that. In government we will stand by that. The tax must be fair.
Second,the tax must be equitable. The Minister of Finance said that in 1984.
Third, the tax ought not to be a tax grab. The Minister of Finance said that in 1984 although he is now perpetrating a tax grab on the Canadians.
Fourth, the minister said and we say that the tax ought to be visible. When people buy something, they ought to know what portion of the cost is for the goods and what portion is for the tax.
These are the four principles that we intend to apply to a federal tax to replace the flawed manufacturers' sales tax. These are just principles, but they are important principles even though they do not say very clearly what kind of tax to implement.
What we are doing now in opposition is not unlike what the Tories did when they were in opposition. One tries various ideas, but one really does not know until one is in government and sees the books whether what one is proposing is completely plausible. Subject to finding out just how bad a situation this crowd leaves us, one of the many good suggestions that we have been promoting with a lot of support is the single tax.
My hon. friend from Broadview-Greenwood has done a lot of work on this. I tell the hon. gentleman from Trois-Rivieres that we are getting a lot of support for that tax right from his own riding and throughout the province of Quebec. Indeed, the support for that tax has probably been most enthusiastic from the province of Quebec in terms of the mail that the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood is getting.
The hon. members opposite shout that that tax is regressive. I think I heard the Minister of State for Finance say that. I want to tell him that that is not what his good friend and my fellow Newfoundlander, Michael Walker who heads up the very conservative think tank at the Fraser Institute in Vancouver, says. He is very supportive of the tax. He says it would be a considerable improvement and light years ahead of the government's proposed goods and services tax.
Michael Walker is one of many hundreds of informed, prominent Canadians who come forward to support this single tax. If the government wants alternatives we could offer all kinds of credible alternatives to what the government is proposing in this goods and services tax.
Let us not forget that what we are debating this afternoon is Bill C-65, an act to provide some borrowing authority for the government so it can rush out and borrow another $25.5 billion to keep afloat for another year. I take the view that borrowing itself is not a sin as long as one borrows within his or her capacity to repay and also, if it is for a reasonable purpose.
These are basically the two yardsticks that prudent individuals apply to themselves when they go out to borrow. They borrow having in mind their ability to repay the indebtedness, and they borrow for a good purpose. In individual terms, it is often a house, a car or any justifiable expenditure. If those two criteria are applied to personal borrowing or government borrowing, there follow a number of questions as to the government's ability to repay or how that ability could be improved. I touched briefly on that point when speaking before Question Period, earlier today. I indicated that the government has within its power changing the interest rate policy of this country.
I happen to think what is going on now is unconscionable. It is unconscionable in terms of what it is doing to the deficit, a matter that is of tremendous concern to people opposite-although one would never know it when one sees what they are doing to the deficit by allowing interest rates to continue very high. It is unconscionable when one realizes that we are fully 5 or
5.5	percentage points above American interest rates. So, the argument of attracting foreign capital does not really apply here. We have already put ourselves in a position that is more than competitive in terms of competing with American loan institutions to attract capital.
It is absolutely unconscionable in what it is doing to family budgets across the country. People who are locked into house mortgages have absolutely no control. They have no say whatsoever when asked to pay that extra $50 to $100 a month over and above what they should be paying. The government has allowed the interest rate to become unconscionably high. People who have consumer loans for cars, for home improvements, for university education, and made those commitments of indebtedness in good faith at a time when interest rates were
May 14, 1990

considerably lower, are now caught, not by any misdemeanour they have committed, but by the terrible insensitivity of the government.
These people all across the country are now paying through the nose, many hundreds of dollars more a month for many families, for their house mortgages, car loans, consumer loans of various kinds, university education loans. They are paying much more than they ought to be paying. If only the government would come up with a fairer and a more sensible interest rate policy or, more to the point, would allow interest rates to fall somewhat.
Of course the government's answer is that it is protecting consumers against themselves. My experience with consumers is that they have more skill and a better track record in protecting themselves well than does the government. Indeed, consumers today would be reasonably well off if they were not saddled with those extra expenditures on mortgages, car loans, and those other expenditures.
Also, when talking about a borrowing bill, one raises the second question that I raised a few moments ago: Are the purposes for which the loan is being made justifiable and reasonable? I am thinking of individual personal consumer borrowing. Once that question is applied to the realm of government, of course, the borrowing is for many, many purposes, but all of which come under the general umbrella of providing hopefully good government for the country.
One must take some particular examples and ask whether the government's expenditure in certain areas is justifiable. I gave a couple of frivolous examples just now to show it was not, but I would like to come to the other side of the question: Is the government, in its stated objective of bringing down the deficit, not cutting in the wrong places, and how can it justify that kind of cut in the light of its request to the House today for another $25.5 billion in borrowing? I think particularly of two examples, and there are many I could give.
Student aid in the country is in an absolutely terrible mess. It is in that kind of a mess because of the frustration which parents and students feel at the gov-
Govemment Orders
ernment for not having upgraded the criteria. These rules determine the amount of living allowance students can claim and the amount that parents are expected to contribute and they have not been changed since 1984. Not since the government took over has it changed the levels, despite the fact we have had some inflation and some increase in the cost of living over those six years. It is common knowledge that in 1990 one cannot buy a commodity for the same price it was six years before. Those people who are trying to get an education with very meagre means, in all parts of the country, are not able to access student aid.
What is student aid? Is it a government hand-out? No. It is a program drawn up by the former Liberal administration and, to its credit, continued by this administration-although a little more stingily, as I have said. It is a program that allows young men and women, who otherwise would not be able to go to university, to access some funding. It is not a government grant. We all know that. It is a loan advanced by the state to those individuals who are required contractually-they signed a contract-to pay back every cent of it with interest.
We are not advocating that there ought to be a Santa Claus approach, that all university education for all people who want it should be given out at no cost to them. Student aid, in effect, just defers the cost to them. It allows them to go to university while they are 17, 18 or 20 years of age and then, when they have some economic power and are employed, they can then pay back those amounts. That seems to me to be a very sensible approach.
That program, as good as it is, is being seriously undermined by the penny-wise, pound-foolish approach of the government. In nickeling and diming away at the deficit, the government sacrifices the university educations of thousands of Canadians from coast to coast.
I was in St. John's a few weeks ago and I attended that massive demonstration of students in post-secondary institutions in St. John's. Students who attend Memorial University of Newfoundland, the Cabot Institute and the Marine Institute came together, several thousand of them, to vent their feelings and to send a message about

May 14, 1990
Government Orders
how the government is hurting them because of the freeze on student aid.
The problem could be cured with a stroke of the pen, but what a beneficial stroke it would be. It would send a signal to thousands of Canadians, young men and women, who are out there now with the knowledge that they are not able to get to university this fall because they cannot afford to go and, under the present rules, they cannot qualify for the necessary funding to go. With one stroke of the pen, the Minister of Finance or the delegated minister could solve this problem by just bringing the rules for student aid, the qualification criteria, up to 1990 standards.
So often in the House we are told, in effect, as I was a few minutes ago, that it is not enough to criticize, and asked: "How would you do it?" Well, I have just said to the minister, to the House and to the government, how we think it should be done. It is very simple. Be fair and apply 1990 guidelines to the student aid program, instead of allowing the 1984 guidelines to stay there. They are not only six years out of date, but are doing some real damage in terms of interfering with the capacity of thousands of Canadians to attend post-secondary education this fall.
I raised that issue as an example of how government spending rules can impact unfavourably or, to put it more bluntly, can hurt ordinary Canadians. There are many other examples.
We know the example of the women's funding issue. The government finally relented on that and agreed to extend the funding for another year. I am delighted to see that my friend, the minister responsible for the status of women is here. I want to say to her that, while the extension of funding took the heat off for the short term, she will owe it to women across Canada, and the cause they stand for, to go to bat to have that funding continued on a permanent basis.
In my riding there are two women's centres, one at Stephenville and one at Port aux Basques. As the minister will know, they have earned a reputation over the years of being among the better women's centres in Canada. I have seen some of the work that they do in terms of coming to the aid of people who are victims of family violence. I could cite some specific examples of
the good work that those women and their organizations have done in those two communities.
I like to think that perhaps one of the reasons that the funding was cut in the first place was that there was not a sufficiently good understanding of the work that was being done by some of those centres. If that is the case, insofar as the two centres I have mentioned are concerned, I am prepared to document for the government some of the examples of what is being done. Members of the House would be encouraged that tax money is being so well spent.
Under the aegis of the debate on this bill, I wish to address the whole issue of regional development, a subject I am sure my friends from rural Quebec would love to hear about. In fact, I would like to hear them talk about the issue because they will know that the policies of this government have devastated the capacity of rural Canada to survive, whether talking about the closing of rural post offices; the closing of rail lines in Newfoundland a year or so ago and now here on the mainland Canada; women's funding, which I mentioned has temporarily got a reprieve so we will not beat that one to death right now in terms of an example; or the cut-backs in ACOA, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency funding.
In many ways the government's record on regional development poses the question: Why should we be voting for this government to borrow more money when it is not spending very well the last borrowings we gave it in the House a year or so ago?
Also, I want to comment on the fisheries aid package that was announced the other day. I wish the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans was here. I understand he is away on business and I am not criticizing him for that, but I do wish he were within the hearing of my voice at this time. I wanted to say to him, as I have said to him privately, that I believe the fish aid package will go some way to addressing some of the problems and easing some of the pain. I have no hesitation in saying that publicly, and I have already said it to him privately.
There are a couple of key issues that it does not address and he acknowledges at least one of these. Let me deal with that one first. It does not address the issue of the inshore fishermen, the so-called fixed gear fishermen. The Minister for International Trade in his re-
